title: Tomorrow we will
goal: Making plans and promises with the little word به — and telling a firm plan from a possibility that's still up in the air.
bekal: express possibility, wishes, and simple conditions

notes: Pashto makes the future with one small word: **به** *ba*. It never changes form, doesn't agree with the doer, and doesn't agree with anything else either. One word for the whole future — much lighter than English "will / going to / shall".

⚠️ The word به doesn't go in front of the verb. It stands **in second place in the sentence**, usually right after the first word — look at these three examples one by one: زه **به** ولاړ شم · سبا **به** ځو · مونږ **به** هلته وخورو. Putting it at the end, or right before the verb, is a mistake people hear at once.

The verb after به almost always takes the completed form from unit 11, so the correct form is زه به **ولاړ** شم, not the plain زه به ځم. The logic is sound — a plan is something you picture as done. If you use the plain form, the meaning shifts to "I will be going", which is rarely what you mean.

The word که means "if", and Pashto conditions use the completed form in the if-clause: که باران **وشي** (if it rains). You don't need the whole range of conditionals yet; the two patterns in the grammar box cover what A1 needs.
The phrase انشاءالله is not a way of dodging. In Pashto it's a fixed part of any sentence about plans, as it is for Muslims everywhere — and leaving it out actually sounds overconfident.
The phrase زنګ وهل means "to phone", literally "to hit the bell". It's one of many verbs built from a noun plus a helper verb, a pattern you've already seen in کار کول and خبرې کول.

grammars.title: One little word for the whole future: به
body: The order is: doer, **به**, thing, completed verb. به never changes, and it never stands at the start of a sentence.

⚠️ If the sentence opens with a time word, به attaches right after it. The correct form is سبا **به** ولاړ شم; the wrong one puts it at the end, as in سبا ولاړ شم به. The rule isn't "after the doer" but "in second place".

grammars.title: Plans, wishes, and possibilities
body: Pashto separates three things that English often lumps under "will" or "might". A firm plan uses **به**; a wish uses **غواړم** plus the base form; a possibility uses **ښایي** or **کېدای شي**.
⚠️ Note that after غواړم the verb takes the **base form without و-**: زه لیکل غواړم. This is one place where the completed prefix must not appear.

sections.title: Making plans, canceling, and arranging things

head: Sentence
Say it
Meaning
rows: I'll let you know the time

blocks.title: Canceling without giving offense
items: Open with an apology: **بخښنه غواړم** *bakhṣəna ghwāṛəm* — "I'm sorry".
Give a short reason, not a long one: **کار راپیدا شو** *kār rāpaydā shū* — "something came up at work". A long excuse sounds made up.
Close with a new offer: **بل ځل به حتماً راشم** *bəl dzal ba hatman rāshəm* — "I'll definitely come next time". This is the part that actually saves the relationship.
⚠️ Don't cancel by text if you can call. In Afghanistan a voice counts for much more than writing, and a written cancellation feels cold.

blocks.title: Ten completed verbs for making plans
items: These ten plus به are enough to plan a whole week. Try it tonight: write seven sentences, one for each day.
